title: The memory model and volatile
sub: Which reorderings are possible, x64 vs ARM64, Volatile.Read/Write
cards/0/title: Order in code is not order in memory
cards/0/body:
In the unit on tasks without await the race was easy to picture: count++ is three steps (read, add, write), and two threads interleave them. There is a subtler problem. Even without shared counters, another thread can see your writes in a different order than you wrote them.

Three parties change the order:

  • the C# compiler — almost never, it does little optimization;
  • the JIT — merges reads, keeps a field in a register, reorders independent operations;
  • the CPU — executes instructions out of order and queues writes in a store buffer before they reach the cache.

All three promise one thing: within one thread the result is as if the code ran strictly in order. They promise nothing about other threads — except what the rules of the memory model guarantee.
cards/1/body:
A classic. One thread spins until a flag is raised, another thread raises it.

The JIT sees that nothing inside the loop changes _stop. So it may read it once before the loop and keep testing a register. For a single thread that is a fair optimization. For two threads it is an endless loop: the other thread did write to memory, but this thread never looks at memory again.

Atomicity has nothing to do with it: a bool is written and read as a whole. The problem is visibility — the read simply is not there. The fix is to read through Volatile.Read(ref _stop) or to put the volatile keyword on the field: the JIT is not allowed to merge such a read or hoist it out of the loop. How they work comes later in this lesson.
cards/1/deep:
In a Debug build and at tier 0 of tiered compilation the JIT barely optimizes, and the code "works". Once a hot method is recompiled at tier 1 (or replaced mid-loop through OSR, on-stack replacement), the read is hoisted out of the loop and the program hangs. That is why the bug shows up "only in Release and only sometimes".

The memory model spec in the dotnet/runtime repository allows this explicitly: adjacent ordinary reads of the same location can be coalesced into one.
cards/2/q: Release build, Run() spins in one thread, a second later another thread calls Stop(). What happens?
cards/2/options/0: It may hang forever: the read of _stop was hoisted out of the loop
cards/2/options/1: It always prints "done": a bool is written atomically
cards/2/options/3: It prints "done", but only after a scheduler quantum
cards/2/explain: Atomicity is not the issue: writing a bool is indeed indivisible. The problem is visibility — the Run thread no longer reads the field from memory, and t.Join() waits forever. The fix is Volatile.Read(ref _stop) or volatile on the field.
cards/2/wrong/1: Atomic means "you will not read half a value". It does not promise the read happens at all.
cards/3/body:
Take two operations on different memory locations. The pairs are: read→read, read→write, write→write, write→read. Which of them the CPU can "swap" as seen from another core depends on the architecture.

  • x64 has a strong model (TSO). Only one reordering is visible: a write followed by a read of another location. The write is still sitting in the buffer while the read already went to the cache.
  • ARM64 has a weak model. All four are possible. That is Apple M-series, Graviton, Ampere, phones.

Hence a nasty class of bugs: code ran for years on x64 servers, and after moving to ARM64 it starts seeing "impossible" states once a day. And the JIT may reorder on its own, on any architecture.
cards/3/deep: TSO is total store order: all cores see writes in a single common order, and a core reads its own not-yet-flushed writes from the buffer (store forwarding). That is why write→read is the only hardware reordering on x64, and only a full fence fixes it: the mfence instruction or any lock-prefixed instruction.
cards/4/q: Which reordering of operations on different locations can an x64 CPU show to another core?
cards/4/options/0: A write, then a read: the read overtakes the write
cards/4/options/3: A read, then a write: the write overtakes the read
cards/4/explain: The write waits in the store buffer while the next read of another location has already executed. x64 does not do the other three — ARM64 does all four.
cards/5/body:
Thread A prepares data and raises a flag. Thread B sees the flag and reads the data. On ARM64, B can see _ready == true but a stale _data == 0: A's writes became visible in reverse order, or B's reads executed in reverse order.

Two promises are needed:

  • the flag write is a release: everything A did before it becomes visible no later than the flag;
  • the flag read is an acquire: everything B does after it will not run earlier.

These are the two methods of the static Volatile class: Volatile.Write(ref field, value) is a write with release, Volatile.Read(ref field) is a read with acquire. There are overloads for all primitive types and references.
cards/6/q: Fix the loop from the start of the lesson without changing the field declaration
cards/6/explain: Volatile.Read cannot be merged with neighboring reads or hoisted out of the loop — the thread looks at memory every time. Volatile.Write makes the write a release. Load and Store are what memory model descriptions and other languages call these operations, but the Volatile class has no methods with those names.
cards/7/title: The volatile keyword and what it does not give you
cards/7/body:
volatile on a field turns every read into Volatile.Read and every write into Volatile.Write. Convenient, but it is easy to forget that the promises end there:

  • no atomicity for compound operations: _count++ on a volatile field is still three steps, increments still get lost;
  • no write→read ordering: a release write and a following acquire read of another location can still swap.

The second one breaks "raise my flag, check the other flag" algorithms. You need a full fence — an operation that no read and no write can cross in either direction. That is Interlocked.Exchange instead of a plain write, or an explicit fence between the lines: Interlocked.MemoryBarrier(), also available as Thread.MemoryBarrier().

And a type restriction: you cannot put volatile on long or double — error CS0677, because on a 32-bit platform writing them is not atomic. For such fields use Volatile.Read and Volatile.Write: they do have overloads for long and double.
cards/7/deep:
volatile is allowed on references, pointers, integers up to 32 bits, bool, char, float, IntPtr/nint and enums based on them. Per the memory model spec, Volatile.Read(ref long) is atomic even on 32 bits.

The old Thread.VolatileRead/VolatileWrite from .NET Framework issued a full fence — they are slower and no longer needed: the Volatile class arrived in .NET Framework 4.5.
cards/8/q: In the code above both fields are volatile and there is no fence. Can you get r1 == 0 and r2 == 0?
cards/8/options/0: Yes: volatile does not stop a read from overtaking an earlier write
cards/8/options/2: Only on ARM64, never on x64
cards/8/options/3: No, if the threads run on different cores
cards/8/explain: A release write holds back what came before it, an acquire read holds back what comes after it. The pair "write, then read" is covered by neither. On x64 it is exactly the one reordering the hardware does. A full fence between the lines in both threads (Interlocked.Exchange instead of the write, or Interlocked.MemoryBarrier) rules this outcome out.
cards/8/wrong/2: The opposite: write→read is exactly what x64 reorders by itself through the store buffer.
cards/9/body:
ECMA-335 promises little. The real runtime (CoreCLR) gives more, and it is written down in the memory model spec in dotnet/runtime:

  • aligned reads and writes up to pointer size are atomic — you never see half a value;
  • a volatile read is an acquire, a volatile write is a release;
  • storing an object reference to a shared location is a release: whoever reads the reference sees the object's fields initialized, without an extra fence;
  • ordering honors data dependency: a read through a reference does not happen before reading the reference itself;
  • Interlocked, Thread.MemoryBarrier and entering/leaving a lock are fences (Interlocked and MemoryBarrier are full ones).

The cost differs by CPU. On x64 a volatile read or write is a plain mov instruction: the hardware already gives acquire and release, and the constraint applies only to the JIT — do not merge, do not reorder. On ARM64 the JIT emits dedicated ldar/stlr instructions (load-acquire and store-release) or a dmb barrier. A full fence costs more everywhere: on x64 it is a lock-prefixed instruction or mfence.
cards/9/deep:
Exactly which instructions the JIT emits on ARM64 depends on its version and the spot in the code: ldar/stlr or a dmb barrier. A full fence on ARM64 is dmb ish.

Note: the "storing a reference is a release" guarantee does not order two independent ordinary writes. If order matters, say so explicitly with Volatile.
cards/10/title: Do you need volatile across await?
cards/10/body:
No. You know from the "Under the hood" unit that the locals of an async method are fields of the state machine, and the continuation after await may run on another thread. So one thread writes memory and another reads it. Still, everything written before await is visible after it.

The reason is the path the continuation takes to the other thread. The task completes by changing its state with Interlocked.CompareExchange, the continuation is put into the pool queue with atomic operations, and the pool thread takes it from the queue atomically too. These are full fences, and they order everything that came before them.

volatile, Volatile and Interlocked are for fields that two threads use at the same time: a stop flag, a counter, publishing an object. When the parts of one chain run in turn through await, the task hands the data over by itself.
cards/11/q: A method writes _total, then does await SaveAsync(), then reads _total. Another pool thread runs the continuation, and nobody else touches _total. Does _total need volatile?
cards/11/options/0: No: completing the task and queuing the continuation are full fences
cards/11/options/1: Yes: the other thread may read a stale value from its core's cache
cards/11/options/3: You need a lock around the read after await
cards/11/explain: One thread wrote, another read — but strictly in turn, with the atomic operations of Task and the pool queue in between. Everything written before await is visible after it. volatile is needed when different threads read and write a field at the same time.
cards/11/wrong/1: Stale values do not come from "its own cache" — the hardware keeps core caches coherent — but from reordering and merging. On the continuation's path the fences rule those out.
cards/12/q: What is true about volatile in C#? Select all.
cards/12/options/0: A long field cannot be declared volatile
cards/12/options/1: _count++ on a volatile field becomes atomic
cards/12/options/2: A read of a volatile field cannot be hoisted out of a loop
cards/12/options/3: A volatile write and a following volatile read of another field can swap places
cards/12/options/4: On x64 every volatile read is a separate fence instruction
cards/12/explain: long is forbidden (CS0677). ++ is still three steps — you need Interlocked. Hoisting is not allowed: every volatile read is real. The write→read pair is not ordered. On x64 a volatile read is a plain mov, the constraints apply to the JIT only.
cards/13/q: Match the operation with what it promises
cards/13/pairs/0/1: Acquire: later operations will not move earlier
cards/13/pairs/1/1: Release: earlier operations will not move later
cards/13/pairs/2/1: A full fence in both directions
cards/13/pairs/3/1: May be merged with a neighbor and hoisted out of a loop
cards/13/pairs/4/0: Storing a reference to a new object
cards/13/pairs/4/1: The reader sees the fields initialized
